newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico almost halved inflation last year.
newsitem.headline: Mexico almost halved inflation last year.

text.p: Mexico said Thursday it cut inflation almost in half in 1996, slowing price rises from 52 percent in 1995 to 27.7 percent last year.
The final figure was lower than some economists had expected, leading analysts to say that local money and stock markets would probably react well when they opened Friday.

But the 1996 inflation number was still well above the government's 20.5 percent target, reflecting the lingering effects of Mexico's economic crisis, which was triggered by a bungled devaluation of the peso in December 1994.

"They did miss their official target but you still have to call the number a success for the central bank," said Gray Newman, an economist at the HSBC James Capel brokerage here. "They nearly cut it in half."
Mexico had enjoyed several years of low inflation until the peso crash, which sent production reeling, prices soaring, cost more than a million jobs and set the economic recovery back several years.
Still struggling to get back on course, President Ernesto Zedillo's government has promised to bring inflation down further this year, to around 15 percent.

Most independent economists believe a figure in the 17- to 19-percent range is more likely -- still on the high side for a country that attained membership of the exclusive OECD club of wealthy nations just before the peso crash.
Alonso Cervera of Mexican brokerage Interacciones said the government was likely to have a harder time bringing down inflation in 1997.
Companies that had not been able to raise prices because of the recession would take advantage of improved sales to fatten their margins, he predicted.
But Mexico's still delicate recovery from recession required a gentle touch on prices, Cervera added.
"Perhaps it's healthier to grow with some inflation than to try and kill inflation in a single blow," he said.
Mexico's inflation last year also looked somewhat high by Latin American standards.
Once the paradise of hyperinflation, with double digit price rises every month the norm in some nations, most of the region has now discovered the joys of low inflation.

Argentina last week announced that prices hardly moved last year, rising just 0.05 of a percentage point. And Brazil, once an inflation junkie, crowed about price rises of 10 percent, its lowest annual figure since 1950.
Among Latin America's big economies only Venezuela, which saw 1996 inflation of 103 percent, had higher price rises than Mexico.
